name: Mohism
info: Mohism was an ancient Chinese philosophy of ethics, logic and technology taught by the followers of Mozi in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; it urged impartial care for all people and opposed offensive war.

facts.thinkers: Mozi (c. 470 BCE – c. 391 BCE), the founder, whose disciples developed the school; the later Mohist logicians, who built on his doctrine; Gongshu Pan, the engineer in the story of the siege of Song, who built machines for the king of Chu; Edward Craig, who prefers the translation “impartial care”; Chris Fraser and Angus C. Graham, modern scholars of the school
facts.texts: the Mozi, the book that embodies the school’s doctrine; the Mohist canon (Mo Jing), on logic, mathematics and the physical sciences; the chapters “Against Music” (非樂) of the Mozi
facts.ideas: impartial care (兼愛, jiān ài, often translated “universal love”); a consequentialist ethics whose goods are order, material wealth and a growing population; appointment by merit, not by family tie; obedience to Tian, Heaven, and belief in spirits; frugality and austerity, including against lavish funerals and music; opposition to offensive war, with defence permitted; the three criteria (San Biao) for testing views, used against fatalism
facts.today: No school or state claims it. Mohism almost disappeared after the Qin dynasty, as it transformed and integrated into sects of Taoism; its logic, science and ethics are studied by modern scholars

t: Mohists taught impartial care: a person should care equally for all others, whatever their relationship, which set them against the Confucians, who held that love should be unconditional but not indiscriminate.

Mohists formed a disciplined organisation with units in all the major kingdoms and became the pre-eminent siege-defence engineers before the Qin unification, opposing offensive war but accepting force in legitimate defence.

Mohism almost disappeared as an independent school after 221 BCE; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy suggests that its more appealing ideas were shared with rival schools by the middle of the former Han dynasty.
dyk: In the story of Gongshu in the Mohist canon, Mozi travelled ten days and nights to Chu, made a wall of his belt and sticks to stand for machines, and showed Gongshu Pan that he could defend Song against any attack; he then announced that three hundred of his disciples were already on Song’s walls, and the king cancelled the invasion.
ev: The Spring and Autumn period begins, the start of the age of the four main philosophic schools that included Mohism
Mozi, the founder of the school, is born
Mozi develops the concept of ai, impartial or universal love, in reaction to Confucianism’s benevolent love
The Qin unification of China ends the wars between states in which Mohist siege-defence skills had been in demand
Jin Guantao, Fan Hongye and Liu Qingfeng argue that Chinese science lacked a definitive structure without a flourishing Mohism

sections.origins:
Mohism was an ancient Chinese philosophy of ethics and logic, rational thought and scientific technology, developed by the scholars who studied under the philosopher Mozi, who lived from about 470 BCE to about 391 BCE. It is embodied in an eponymous book, the Mozi. It arose at about the same time as Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism, and was one of the four main philosophic schools of the period from around 770 to 221 BCE, the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. In that time Mohism was seen as a major rival to Confucianism.

Mozi developed the concept of ai, usually rendered as love, in the 4th century BCE as a reaction to Confucianism’s benevolent love. He tried to replace what he considered a long-entrenched Chinese over-attachment to family and clan. Other features of his thought answered conditions of his age: war and famine were common, and it is suggested that Mozi spoke against lavish funerals and music in response to the Zhou king and the aristocrats, who spent great time on delicate music while ordinary peasants could hardly meet their subsistence needs.

The Mohists also formed a structured organisation, a network of local units in all the major kingdoms made up of both the scholarly and the working classes, each led by a juzi, literally “chisel”, who appointed his own successor.
sections.ideas:
Mohism is best known for the concept popularly translated as “universal love” (兼愛, jiān ài). According to Edward Craig, “impartial care” is the more accurate translation, because Mozi was more concerned with ethics than with morality. A person should care equally for all other individuals, whatever their relationship to them, and the Mohists held that all people are equally deserving of material benefit and protection from harm. Morality was defined not by tradition and ritual but by a constant guide that parallels utilitarianism, one that promotes behaviour maximising the general utility of all the people in a society.

The basic goods in this consequentialist thinking, in the words quoted from a modern scholar, are order, material wealth and an increase in population. Mozi posited that conflict arises from the absence of moral uniformity, so leaders were to be chosen who would surround themselves with righteous followers and create a hierarchy that harmonises what is right and wrong, with conformity in speech and behaviour expected of all. This model leaves no freedom of speech, but subjects were required to report all things good or bad to their rulers. Mozi opposed nepotism and held that an incapable officer should be demoted, even a relative of the ruler. Mohism was opposed to any aggression, especially war between states, though a state might use force in legitimate defence.

Mohists believed in Heaven (Tian) as a divine force, in spirits that knew of the immoral acts of men and punished them, and in austerity in life and government.
sections.spread:
Mohism was popular in early China. The Mohists were often hired by the warring kingdoms as advisors to the state, and like the Confucians they hired out their services not only for gain but to realise their own ethical ideals. In this they resembled the other wandering philosophers and knights-errant of the period. They believed in aiding the defensive warfare of smaller Chinese states against the offensive warfare of larger domineering states.

Within each unit of the organisation a frugal and ascetic lifestyle was enforced. The Mohists developed the sciences of fortification and statecraft and wrote treatises on government, from efficient agricultural production to the laws of inheritance. Their understanding of mathematics and the physical sciences, combined with an anti-militarist philosophy and the skills of artisans, made them the pre-eminent siege-defence engineers before the Qin unification of China, and followers were employed for their ability as negotiators and as defence engineers.

One offshoot that has received some attention is the School of Names, which was interested in resolving logical puzzles. Little of its writing survives, since problems of logic were deemed trivial by most later Chinese philosophers. Joseph Needham saw the group as developing a precursor philosophy of science that was never fully developed, while others believe that calling these Logicians proto-scientists reveals too much modern bias.
sections.power:
Mohism was not the doctrine of a state, and its record in practice is that of its organisation and its engineers. Mozi and his disciples worked concertedly and systematically to invent and synthesise measures of benefit to defence, including defensive arms and strategy, and their corresponding logistics and military mobilisation. Many were applied and remained an aspect of military affairs throughout history. The Mozi is highly respected by modern scholars and ranks as a classic on military matters on a par with Sunzi’s Art of War, the former on defensive strategy, the latter on offensive strategy.

The story of Gongshu in the Mohist canon dramatises this work. When Mozi heard that Gongshu Pan had built machines for the king of Chu to use in an invasion of the smaller state of Song, he travelled ten days and nights to Chu, made a wall of his belt and sticks to stand for the machines, and showed that he could defend Song against any offensive strategy of Chu. He announced that three hundred of his disciples were already on the walls of Song, and the king cancelled the invasion.

The Mohist canon also described many fields of physical science and gave a small wealth of information on mathematics, with definitions of the point, parallels, circumference, diameter, radius and volume.
sections.critiques:
Mohist impartiality was a target of attack by other Chinese philosophical schools, most notably the Confucians, who believed that while love should be unconditional it should not be indiscriminate: children, for example, should hold a greater love for their parents than for random strangers. The Mohists answered that people in principle should care for all people equally and that love should be offered without regard to reciprocation.

Modern readers have raised other doubts. The unity in belief and speech Mozi sought was meant to unite people and avoid sectarianism, but that in a situation of corruption and tyranny the teaching might be misused as a tool for oppression. The Mohist model also has no freedom of speech. The Mohists were wary of more atheistic thinkers of the time, such as Han Fei, and, given the vague nature of the records, the Mohist scribes themselves may not have been clear about spirits.

Mozi argued against fatalism, which he blamed for poverty and suffering, using three criteria: history, the experiences of common people and usefulness in law or politics. He also took whole chapters, titled “Against Music”, to argue that the fine arts had no utility in governing or for the common people. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls the distinctively Mohist package of economic and cultural views, including its parsimony and its rejection of music and ritual, harsh and unappealing.
sections.legacy:
With the unification of China under the Qin after 221 BCE, China was no longer divided into states constantly fighting one another, and the Mohist skill in defending cities in siege wars was no longer needed. Mohism almost disappeared as an independent school of thought, transformed and integrated into sects of Taoism. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives a further reason: that as a social and philosophical movement Mohism gradually collapsed into irrelevance, since by the middle of the former Han dynasty its more appealing aspects were shared with rival schools. Its core ethical doctrines had largely been absorbed into Confucianism in a modified and unsystematic form, and the difficult, dense texts of the later Mohist Canons quickly became corrupt.

Modern scholars have drawn lessons from its fate. Jin Guantao, Fan Hongye and Liu Qingfeng have argued that without the influence of the proto-scientific precepts of Mohism, Chinese science lacked a definitive structure. They hold that had Mohism, rich in scientific thought, grown and strengthened in the Eastern Han period, when Han studies of the Confucian classics were declining, conditions might have favoured a scientific structure, but that this did not happen.

Mohism has been set beside later ideas of ethics: its tenets of altruism and utilitarianism link it to the subjects of Consequentialism, Buddhist ethics and Effective altruism, and the book Mozi remains the text that embodies its doctrine.

summary: Mohism was an ancient Chinese school founded on the teaching of Mozi, built on impartial care for all people, merit in government and opposition to offensive war. Its organised followers became the foremost siege-defence engineers of their day, and the school almost disappeared after the Qin unification of 221 BCE.
references: Chris Fraser, The Philosophy of the Mozi: The First Consequentialists (Columbia University Press, 2016)
Angus C. Graham, Later Mohist Logic, Ethics and Science (The Chinese University Press, 2004)
Angus C. Graham, Disputers of the Tao: Philosophical Argument in Ancient China (Open Court, 1993)
Philip J. Ivanhoe and Brian W. Van Norden, eds., Readings in Classical Chinese Philosophy (Hackett, 2001)
notes: Start -470 circa true: the article gives Mozi c. 470 BC – c. 391 BC and says the concept of Ai was developed in the 4th century BC; these overlap loosely (470–391 mostly lies in the 5th century), so I used his birth year as hedged and kept the 4th-century statement as the article words it.
End -221 circa true: the article says Mohism almost disappeared 'after 221 BC' and that by the middle of the former Han dynasty its appeal was shared by rivals; no firm end year.
Event 1996 is the publication year of Jin, Fan and Liu in the article's source list; the article gives no event dates otherwise.
The article says 'one of the four main philosophic schools from around 770–221 BC' while listing Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism, with Mohism: left as the article gives it.
Left out: the seven disasters of an unrighteous ruler (listed in the article, not needed), early marriage and the sacrifices of bulls and rams, Brecht's Me-ti and the German-language further reading.
'Effective altruism' appears only in the article's See also list; the 'today' fact says only that.
The article's text on fatalism contains a garbled sentence ('the western view of sinfulness'); I left that sentence out.
In 'power' the article describes no state ruled by Mohism; the section reports the organisation's defensive work instead.
Wording in the quotations of Mozi's three criteria and the 'Against Music' chapters follows the article's list.
